dialogs.title: Dialogue — Har du vært der?
dialogs.intro: The common room, in the evening. Ingrid opens her laptop and turns the screen toward Budi. On it is a photo of a green sky over snowy mountains.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.id: Have you ever seen the northern lights?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nei, aldri. Jeg har bodd her i bare fire måneder.
lines.id: No, never. I've only lived here for four months.
lines.literal: no, never. I have lived here in only four months.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Da må du reise nordover. Har du vært utenfor Oslo i det hele tatt?
lines.id: Then you have to go north. Have you been outside Oslo at all?
lines.literal: then must you travel north-ward. have you been outside Oslo in the whole taken?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg har vært i Bergen én gang. Jeg reiste dit i forrige måned.
lines.id: To Bergen once. I went there last month.
lines.literal: I have been in Bergen one time. I travelled there in last month.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Det teller ikke. Bergen er bare Oslo med mer regn.
lines.id: That doesn't count. Bergen is just Oslo with more rain.
lines.literal: it counts not. Bergen is only Oslo with more rain.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Have you lived in Northern Norway?

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Jeg bodde i Tromsø i to år. Jeg jobbet på et hotell der.
lines.id: I lived in Tromsø for two years. I worked at a hotel there.
lines.literal: I lived in Tromsø in two years. I worked at a hotel there.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Mørkt i to måneder. Men jeg har aldri sett noe vakrere.
lines.id: Dark for two months. But I've never seen anything more beautiful.
lines.literal: dark in two months. but I have never seen something more-beautiful.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Mange ganger. Har du prøvd det?
lines.id: Many times. Have you tried it?
lines.literal: many times. have you tried it?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nei, men jeg har lest om det. Det holder foreløpig.
lines.id: No, but I've read about it. That'll do for now.
lines.literal: no, but I have read about it. that holds meanwhile.

notes: **This form is built from two parts: *har* + the third form of the verb.** *Har sett*, *har bodd*, *har vært*, *har spist*. *Har* never changes, and the third form never changes — so there's only one form per verb to learn.
**When do you use it?** When you talk about **experience** (ever or never) or a **result you can still feel now**. When you say **exactly when** something happened, use the simple past.

**Look at the fourth line of the dialogue**: *Jeg **har vært** i Bergen én gang* (experience, no time) and then *Jeg **reiste** dit i forrige måned* (time given, so simple past). The two forms sit side by side in one answer, and that's exactly the pattern you'll meet most.
**Jeg har bodd her i fire måneder** — this form is also used for something that **started in the past and is still going on**. English does exactly the same: "I have lived here for four months".

**Nordlys** (literally "north light") is the aurora borealis. It can be seen from late September to late March, and the farther north, the more often. In Oslo it's rare; in Tromsø it can appear several times a week.
**I det hele tatt** means "at all, in general". A very common fixed phrase that can't be translated word for word.

grammars.title: Forming the third verb form
body: The groups are exactly the same as for the past tense in unit 15 — so there's no new split to learn, just new endings.
after: Group 1 is easiest: the third form is **exactly the same** as the past. *Snakket* is used for both, and the context tells them apart.
Group 2 drops the final *e*: *spiste* → *spist*, *leste* → *lest*, *kjøpte* → *kjøpt*. A tidy pattern.
Groups 3 and 4 also just drop the *-e*: *levde* → *levd*, *bodde* → *bodd*. So the whole system boils down to: **drop the -e from the past form**, except group 1, which doesn't change.

grammars.title: Strong verbs: the third form
body: Strong verbs must be learned in all three forms at once. Say each row in one breath — *er, var, vært* — just as you once learned *go, went, gone*.
after: ⚠️ *Å si* → *sagt* is pronounced **sahkt**, with the *g* turning into a *k*. The same goes for *å legge* → *lagt* → **lahkt**. Two very common words with misleading spelling.
Notice how many third forms end in *-tt* or *-t*: *hatt, gått, tatt, fått, gitt, sett, vært*. If you're unsure, *-tt* is a good guess for short strong verbs.

grammars.title: Har vært versus var
body: This is a choice you'll make in almost every sentence when telling a story. The rule boils down to one question: **are you saying when?**

head: Use *har* + third form for…
Example
Use the simple past for…
Example
rows: *Jeg har bodd her i fire år.*

after: A practical rule that rarely fails: **if the sentence contains *i går*, *i fjor*, *klokka fem*, *forrige uke* — use the simple past.** If there's no time expression at all, it's almost always the *har* form.
Good news for English speakers: this is the same split as English "I have been" versus "I was", so your instinct is usually right: *har du vært?* = "have you been?", *jeg har spist* = "I have eaten".

blocks.text: These questions come up in almost every getting-to-know-you conversation that lasts more than five minutes. Learn the form; the content can be swapped.

head: Norsk
English
rows: Have you been to Norway before?
Have you ever seen the northern lights?
How long have you lived here?

blocks.text: Notice that *ikke*, *aldri* and *nettopp* still sit in slot four — between *har* and the third form. The order is exactly the same as the helping-verb pattern from unit 8: *jeg har **ikke** sett*, *jeg har **aldri** spist*.
Vocabulary for talking about places — an endless topic of conversation in a country with fewer people than many single cities, but stretching longer than the distance from Oslo to Rome.

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Write five sentences about places you've **been** with *har vært*, then five sentences about **when** you went there, in the simple past.
Take ten strong verbs from the table and say all three forms in a row, out loud: *er, var, vært — går, gikk, gått — tar, tok, tatt*.
Finally: ask yourself about five experiences with *har du noen gang…?* and answer them all, half with *ja* and half with *nei, aldri*.
